subtitulo: No very, no thing, no get — at the counter
descripcion: Advanced English is limited less by what the speaker does not know than by what they reach for first. *Very*, *good*, *bad*, *thing*, *a lot*, *nice*, *interesting*, *make*, *get* and *big* cover an enormous amount of ground badly. Replacing them forces retrieval of vocabulary already known but inaccessible under time pressure. This week the words are simply banned.

cuadroReferencia.titulo: The ten banned words and where to go instead
filas: Is there one stronger adjective? *very tired* → *exhausted*
Say what made it so — natives hear this as negative

ejemplos.texto: *It was bland rather than bad — just forgettable.*
*The sauce was rich without being cloying.*
*Rice is a staple there, not a side dish.*
*The prices were eye-watering for what arrived.*
*It's an acquired taste, and I haven't acquired it.*

notas: *Very + adjective* usually means a stronger single adjective exists.
Precision is not formality. *Bland* and *stodgy* are everyday words, just specific ones.
*Thing* is almost always avoidable and almost always worth avoiding in writing.

es.en: Spanish leans on *muy* + adjective exactly as English leans on *very*, and both languages have the stronger single word available. The habit transfers directly; so does the fix.
es.es: El español recurre a «muy» + adjetivo igual que el inglés recurre a «very», y ambos idiomas disponen de una palabra más fuerte. El hábito se transfiere directamente, y también la solución.

de.en: German sehr + adjective works exactly like very + adjective, and German also has the stronger single words (eiskalt – freezing). The habit transfers directly, and so does the fix.
de.de: «Sehr» + Adjektiv funktioniert genau wie «very» + Adjektiv, und auch im Deutschen gibt es stärkere Einzelwörter («eiskalt» – «freezing»). Sowohl die Gewohnheit als auch die Lösung lassen sich direkt übertragen.

it.en: Italian often intensifies with -issimo (bellissimo, stanchissimo), which tends to become very beautiful or very tired. English prefers a stronger single word (stunning, exhausted).
it.it: L'italiano intensifica spesso con «-issimo» («bellissimo», «stanchissimo»), che tende a diventare «very beautiful» o «very tired». L'inglese preferisce una parola unica più forte («stunning», «exhausted»).

fr.en: French très or vraiment + adjective works like very + adjective, and French also has stronger single words (épuisé – exhausted). The habit transfers directly, and so does the fix.
fr.fr: «Très» ou «vraiment» + adjectif fonctionne comme «very» + adjectif, et le français dispose aussi de mots plus forts («épuisé» – «exhausted»). L'habitude se transfère, et la solution aussi.

pt.en: Portuguese intensifies with muito or -íssimo (cansadíssimo), which tends to become very tired. English prefers a stronger single word (exhausted).
pt.pt: O português intensifica com «muito» ou «-íssimo» («cansadíssimo»), o que tende a virar «very tired». O inglês prefere uma palavra única mais forte («exhausted»).

errores: Swapping an overused word for an obscure one. *Comestible* is no improvement on *edible*.

es: *importante* rendered as *important* for size: *an important amount* instead of *a considerable* or *large amount*.
de: *spannend* rendered as *exciting* for every interesting topic, which overstates it: *an exciting report* instead of *an interesting report*.
it: *importante* rendered as *important* for size: *an important sum* instead of *a considerable* or *large sum*.
fr: *important* for size carried over: *an important sum* instead of *a considerable* or *large sum*.
pt: *importante* rendered as *important* for size: *an important amount* instead of *a considerable* or *large amount*.

mision.consigna: Write a complaint-free account of a recent dealing with an office or a service provider, as if for a friend who's about to do the same.
requisitos: none of the banned words: *very, good, bad, thing, a lot, nice, interesting, make, get, big*
three precise adjectives you had to search for
use *red tape*, *customer service* and *to fill in the form*
one sentence with *to be sent from pillar to post*

microtareas.texto: Take a real email you wrote this week. Circle every banned word and replace it.
Describe the last time you *got put on hold* in five sentences — no *very*, no *bad*.
Record 90 seconds on *red tape* in your country. Replay it and count the banned words.

autochequeo: Search the text for each of the ten. Zero hits?
Any word precise but too obscure for the register?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on lexical precision. (1) Flag every banned word that got through. (2) Flag every vague adjective and give two precise alternatives. (3) Flag anything precise but too obscure for the register. (4) Say which three sentences are strongest and why. Do not rewrite the text.
